title: Damon Stands Surety for Pythias
text:
The story was told by Aristoxenus, who said he heard it from Dionysius himself, the tyrant of Syracuse, after his fall. Damon and Phintias (later called Pythias) were two followers of Pythagoras living in Syracuse in the 4th century BC. Courtiers of Dionysius, wanting to test how far the famous loyalty of the Pythagoreans went, had Phintias accused of plotting against the tyrant and condemned to death.

Phintias asked for the rest of the day to settle his affairs and those of Damon, his friend and partner. He offered Damon as surety. Damon agreed to stay in his place and die if Phintias did not come back. The courtiers laughed and expected that Damon had been made a fool.

As evening approached, Phintias returned to face his execution. Dionysius was so struck that he released both men and asked to be admitted as a third member of their friendship. According to the account, they declined. Cicero, Diodorus and Iamblichus all repeated the story, and Damon and Pythias became the classic pair of faithful friends in later literature.
lesson: Keep your word to a friend even when breaking it would save you. That kind of faithfulness is rare enough to move even people who believe no one can be trusted.
source: Aristoxenus, quoted in Iamblichus, Life of Pythagoras 33; Cicero, De Officiis 3.45; Diodorus Siculus, Library 10.4
caveat: Ancient versions differ on which Dionysius was involved and on details of the test, and the story may be partly embellished.
